script:
Did you know that the first human-made object to reach space did not actually stay there? It was a German rocket launched in nineteen forty-four that poked its head into the void and fell straight back down. Today, we are exploring how we went from those first vertical leaps to building permanent bases on the moon.

That nineteen forty-four flight was just a sub-orbital test, but it proved space was reachable. It was not until nineteen forty-nine that the Bumper-W-A-C reached even higher, over two hundred and forty miles up. This raised a huge question: how do we get something to actually stay in orbit instead of falling back to Earth?

The answer came in nineteen fifty-seven with Sputnik One, a small metal sphere that used an R-seven rocket to reach orbital velocity. It did not just sit there; it sent back radio beeps that helped scientists study the density of our ionosphere. If a simple machine could survive the vacuum, could a person do the same?

We found out just four years later when Yuri Gagarin became the first human to orbit our planet in nineteen sixty-one. This sparked a massive competition between the Soviet Union and the United States, culminating in the historic nineteen sixty-nine moon landing. But once we reached the moon, did the competition just keep heating up?

Actually, the focus shifted from one-off flights to building a permanent presence through cooperation. The International Space Station, built between nineteen ninety-eight and twenty-eleven, became a laboratory where countries worked together instead of against each other. But as government budgets changed, people started asking: could a private company do this better?

Enter SpaceX, which in two thousand eight became the first private company to launch a liquid-fueled rocket into orbit. They did not just want to reach space; they wanted to make it affordable by landing and reusing their rockets. This leads us to wonder: exactly how much has the scale of space travel changed since those early days?

The change has been staggering, with companies now launching multiple times per week. By May of twenty-twenty-six, Falcon nine rockets were averaging about three missions every single week, and their boosters had completed hundreds of landings. With so many launches, are we spending all our time just looking back at our own planet?

While we use satellites for internet and observation, we are also looking deeper into the universe than ever before. Since the Hubble Space Telescope launched in nineteen ninety, we have confirmed over five thousand exoplanets in our galaxy. This raises the ultimate question: if there are trillions of galaxies out there, when are we going back to live among the stars?

The answer lies in the twenty-twenties with two massive global programs aiming for the moon. The United States is leading the Artemis program to build a base camp, while China leads the International Lunar Research Station. However, building a home on another world is incredibly difficult and full of risks we are still learning to manage.

Before we look toward our future on the moon, let us see if you remember the pioneer who started the human journey. Who was the very first person to leave our atmosphere and successfully orbit the Earth?

We have come a long way from nineteen forty-four. We moved from simple test rockets to orbiting satellites, then to putting humans on the moon, and now toward private companies making space access a weekly occurrence. Our journey into the stars is really just beginning, and the moon is our next big stepping stone.
